title: Reading differently with ChatGPT: EFL learners’ use of Question-Answer Relationship strategy
extended_summary:
This paper examines how university English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learners developed reading comprehension when using ChatGPT together with the Question-Answer Relationship (QAR) strategy. The core research question was how learners’ reading comprehension changed through this integration, especially across different QAR levels: locating explicit information, synthesizing across text segments, and making inferences about tone and author intent. The study addresses a practical problem in EFL reading instruction: students often need individualized support with vocabulary, sentence structure, and higher-order comprehension, but traditional instruction may not provide timely, adaptive scaffolding.

The intervention combined structured reading strategy instruction through QAR with guided use of ChatGPT. Students completed five weekly guided reading sessions in which they read texts, answered TOEFL-style comprehension questions, generated their own QAR questions and answers, asked ChatGPT to generate questions, and then compared, revised, and discussed responses through free-form interaction. The study used three rounds of semi-structured interviews across five weeks and analyzed 105 interviews thematically using the QAR framework categories (Right There, Think and Search, Author and You) alongside inductive coding.

Participants were 35 first-year undergraduate students in an academic English program at a university in northern China. They were enrolled in two EFL classes per week and also completed one guided ChatGPT-supported reading practice session per week. Most participants self-identified as low-intermediate in TOEFL-related reading proficiency and had limited prior experience with generative AI. Interviews were conducted in Chinese, transcribed, translated, and coded in NVivo.

The main conclusion is that learners described a developmental progression in comprehension: ChatGPT first helped them identify explicit information and understand vocabulary and sentence structure, then supported summarizing and synthesizing across paragraphs, and finally helped them engage in inferential and interpretive reading about tone, stance, and author intention. Students did not simply accept ChatGPT outputs passively; many used it dialogically to compare reasoning and refine their own understanding. At the same time, participants identified limitations in ChatGPT, including weak handling of polysemous vocabulary, unclear parsing of long sentences, overlong summaries, and sometimes inaccurate inferential explanations. The authors conclude that ChatGPT can be a useful reading partner when paired with structured strategy instruction, but its value depends on critical, strategic use and AI literacy.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI’s conversational large language model used for interactive language support, explanation, and question-answering.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as a reading comprehension assistant alongside the Question-Answer Relationship (QAR) strategy in guided EFL reading sessions. Students submitted texts to ChatGPT, asked it to generate QAR-type questions, requested translations/explanations, compared its answers with their own, and used it dialogically to clarify vocabulary, sentence structure, summaries, and inferences.

findings.finding_summary: In qualitative interviews, participants reported that ChatGPT supported surface-level reading comprehension by helping them locate explicit information, understand vocabulary in context, and break down difficult sentences during Right There question work. The study describes a developmental progression in comprehension support across five weeks, but reports no quantitative effect size or test-score outcome. Sample included 35 first-year university EFL learners (105 interviews).
findings.measure: Self-reported reading comprehension development in locating explicit information, vocabulary understanding, and sentence-level comprehension from semi-structured interviews

findings.finding_summary: Participants reported that ChatGPT supported higher-level comprehension during Think and Search tasks by prompting synthesis across paragraphs, summarization of main ideas, and understanding of text logic such as sequencing and cause-effect relations. Findings are based on thematic analysis of learner interviews rather than direct performance measures. Sample included 35 students and 105 interviews.
findings.measure: Self-reported development of synthesis, summarization, and discourse-level comprehension from semi-structured interviews

findings.finding_summary: Learners reported that ChatGPT, combined with QAR, helped deepen interpretive reading through Author and You questions, including inference, tone analysis, author-intent interpretation, and forming personal views about texts. The paper frames this as improved critical reading and interpretive confidence, but does not report standardized reading outcomes or effect sizes. Sample included 35 first-year university EFL learners.
findings.measure: Self-reported inferencing, tone/intent interpretation, and critical reading development from semi-structured interviews

findings.finding_summary: The study reports that students used ChatGPT dialogically rather than passively, and that this process supported learner autonomy, metacognitive reflection, strategic thinking, and critical engagement with texts. These conclusions come from thematic analysis of interview data collected across one month, with no quantitative scale scores reported. Sample included 35 students across 105 interviews.
findings.measure: Self-reported learner autonomy, metacognitive awareness, and strategic thinking from semi-structured interviews

findings.finding_summary: Participants also identified limitations in ChatGPT’s reading support: vague handling of polysemous vocabulary without sufficient context, unclear parsing of long sentences, overly extractive summaries, and sometimes inaccurate or weakly explained inferential responses. Thus, the paper presents ChatGPT as useful but inconsistent, requiring strategic prompting and user evaluation. Sample included 35 learners.
findings.measure: Learner-reported limitations in vocabulary explanation, sentence parsing, summarization, and inferential reasoning from semi-structured interviews

quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical qualitative study with a clearly described intervention context and repeated semi-structured interviews, but it does not include a control group, quantitative outcome measures, or causal identification. Evidence is therefore informative but below experimental or quasi-experimental standards.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports positive perceived impacts on reading comprehension and learner autonomy, but impact is based on qualitative self-report with no effect sizes or standardized outcome data. As a result, magnitude of impact remains unclear.
